title: Polonnaruwa (1968)
hookLine: before the great stone Buddhas in Sri Lanka he describes a clarity he'd long sought

cards: Autumn 1968. After twenty-seven years as a monk, Thomas Merton is given leave for a long journey abroad.
He flies to Asia: Bangkok, then India, up into the Himalayan foothills, where he meets the Dalai Lama three times and they talk about prayer and meditation.
Then, in early December, Sri Lanka, and an ancient ruined city called Polonnaruwa, where huge figures of the Buddha are carved straight into a wall of granite.
He takes off his shoes and walks up to them across the wet grass. And something happens there that, he'll write, makes his whole Asian journey come clear.

teach.b: First, the place. Polonnaruwa was a royal capital of Sri Lanka about nine hundred years ago.
At a site called Gal Vihara, craftsmen cut enormous figures out of a single granite outcrop: the Buddha seated in meditation, a tall standing figure, and the Buddha lying on his side, at peace.
They're still there, weathered, calm, open to the sky. Second, what Merton saw.

teach.h: JERKED OUT OF HIS USUAL SEEING.
teach.b: In his journal, published after his death as The Asian Journal, he wrote that, looking at those faces, he was suddenly jerked out of his habitual way of seeing.
Everything became clear, obvious and simple: the rock, the figures, the sky. He felt he'd seen what he'd been obscurely looking for all his life. Third, what it wasn't.
He was a Catholic monk on that grass, and he died one, just over a week later. He was grateful to the Buddhist tradition for the beauty and stillness of that place, and received the moment as a gift.
Buddhists and Catholics would each describe that clarity in their own words, and it's worth not blurring them. Fourth, the Catholic thread. Scripture talks about seeing, too.
Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God."

teach.h: THROUGH A GLASS, THEN FACE TO FACE.
teach.b: And Paul: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face."

teach.h: BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.
teach.b: For Merton, Polonnaruwa was a glimpse through the glass: a moment of clean-hearted seeing, the kind contemplation had been preparing him for since that first mosaic in Rome.

how: Catholic contemplatives speak of a simple, loving gaze in prayer, and many Catholics practice it by looking long at an icon, a crucifix, the Blessed Sacrament or creation.

games.q: you're a Catholic monk standing barefoot before great stone figures of the Buddha, and everything suddenly becomes clear. what do you do with it?
o: leave your monastery and your faith
receive it as a gift and write it down honestly
ignore it; it's not your tradition
games.why: Merton wrote it down in his journal, saying his whole Asian journey had come clear, and remained a Catholic monk.

practice: Choose one thing to look at, a tree outside, a photo of someone you love, the grain of a table, your own hand, and keep looking past the point where you'd usually move on.
When your eyes want to leave, bring them back, and let it be exactly what it is, no commentary. If you pray, let the looking be your prayer.
